identification: One of three difficult-to-identify Gallinago snipes in Singapore. From Common Snipe, most obviously differentiated by a lack of clear white trailing edge to the secondaries, shorter bill and larger-headed appearance (see that species for more differences). Apart from a long list of overlapping and weakly defined separation features, only truly differentiable from Swinhoe's Snipe with a clear view of the spread tail (or measurements in the hand). This species has one (vs. more than one in Swinhoe's) intermediate-width feather between the wide central tail feathers and the 6-9 pin-like feathers on the outer-tail. These feathers are referred to as "pins" as they are extremely narrow, less than 2 mm wide. On Swinhoe's, only the outermost pair of tail feathers are narrow (varying from 2 to 4 mm wide), while the rest gradually increase in width towards the central feathers (giving the impression of at least two intermediate-width tail feathers outside the central few, while Pin-tailed shows only one when tail is fully spread). identification: Also known as the Arctic Skua, this is a medium sized Jaeger, smaller and slimmer than Pomarine Jaeger, lacking the heavy, barrel-chested build of that species. Can occur in light and dark colour morphs. On the breeding plumage of the light morph, the face and cap are black, upperparts are dark brown/grey except for a pale yellow band wrapping around the nape to the sides of head. Underparts are white except for a brown breast band (sometimes indistinct) and a dark vent. The rarer dark morph simply appears grey or brown all over. Breeding adults have elongated central tail feathers extending beyond the other rectrices, but these elongated feathers are not twisted as in Pomarine Jaeger. Non-breeding adults and immatures become barred all over, but the extent of barring may vary. Parasitic Jaeger shows prominent white at the bases of the primaries on the underwing appearing as a broad single white panel, but lacks this white panel on the upperwing. The outer 4-6 primaries on the upperwing show prominently white shafts, fewer than Pomarine Jaeger. SIMILAR SPECIES Long-tailed Jaeger Stercorarius longicaudus Pomarine Jaeger Stercorarius pomarinus

identification: Also known as the Long-tailed Skua, this is the smallest and most slender of the three Jaegers. On the breeding plumage of the light morph, the face and cap are black, upperparts are dark brown/grey except for a pale yellow band wrapping around the nape to the sides of head. Black flight feathers and a black trailing edge on the secondaries also contrast with the dark brown/grey upperside. On the underside, the breast is white, fading into dark grey on the from the belly and the underwings onwards. Breeding adults have massively elongated central tail feathers, much longer than the other two Jaegers. Non-breeding adults and immatures appear heavily scaled on the wings, with a variable amount of mottling or dark colouration over the rest of the body. Only the outer 2 primaries show prominently white shafts, fewer than Parasitic and Pomarine Jaeger. SIMILAR SPECIES Pomarine Jaeger Stercorarius pomarinus Parasitic Jaeger Stercorarius parasiticus

Red-throated Pipit at Sembawang Road

identification: Adult has heavily streaked upperparts including back, rump, and uppertail-coverts, with prominent blackish streaks/spotting on breast and flanks, and pinkish-red head-sides, throat, and upper breast. Reddish coloration on the head is less extensive on autumn/winter birds and females, and absent in juveniles. photos.caption: Black-headed Bunting at Neo Tiew Harvest Place
Black-headed Bunting at Neo Tiew Harvest Place

identification: Male in breeding plumage has a distinctive black head, chestnut upperparts, and bright yellow underparts; non-breeding male is similar but head feathers have sandy fringes. Challenging to separate females and juveniles from Red-headed Bunting, another species which could possibly occur as a vagrant to Singapore. Females and first-winter birds are very similar to that species, and often inseparable in the field; on average the crown is more streaked, rump less yellow, bill larger, and primary projection longer.
